transcript.text: Every time I put the oven on it runs for a few minutes and then the trip switch goes and half the house loses power. Reset it 3 times tonight. Hotpoint built-in, about 9 years old. What could cause this?

## Most likely cause: a failing heating element

On a 9-year-old oven, the classic culprit is a heating element breaking down internally. Elements have a metal sheath with insulation packed around the wire inside. Over time, cracks let moisture in, and when the element heats up, current leaks from the wire to the earthed casing. That earth leakage trips the RCD.

The pattern you describe fits this well:
• Runs a few minutes, then trips: the element expands as it heats, and the fault only appears once it's hot.
• Half the house goes off: your consumer unit is likely a split-load board, where one RCD (residual current device) protects several circuits. An RCD trips on earth leakage, not overload, so everything on that side goes down together.

Quick check: look at which switch actually flips down in the consumer unit. If it's the larger RCD switch (usually with a "T" test button), that points strongly to earth leakage, i.e. an element or other component leaking to earth. If only the cooker's own MCB trips, that's more like a short circuit or overload.

## Other possible causes
• Fan motor (on fan ovens): worn or water-damaged motors can leak to earth.
• Damaged wiring or terminal block at the back of the oven: heat damage, loose or scorched connections.
• Grill element: it fails just as often as the oven element.
• Moisture from cleaning, spills, or steam getting into components.
• Less likely: the cooker isolation switch, the supply cable, or a sensitive or ageing RCD (but if it only happens with the oven, the oven is the prime suspect).

## Narrowing it down
If your oven has separate functions, try each one on its own and see which trips:
• Grill only → grill element
• Conventional (top/bottom heat) → top or bottom element
• Fan oven → rear circular element or fan motor
• Light/fan only, no heat → fan motor or wiring

That tells you, or an engineer, where to look and can save diagnostic time.

## Safety
• Stop resetting it repeatedly. The RCD is doing its job by detecting current going where it shouldn't.
• Turn the oven off at the cooker isolation switch (the big red switch on the wall) until it's sorted, so you can restore power to the rest of the house.
• If you see scorch marks, smell burning, or the switch or socket feels hot, leave it off and get it looked at.

## Fixing it
• Elements are cheap, typically £15–40 for a Hotpoint. The rear fan element is often a fairly simple swap: remove the back panel inside the oven, unscrew the element, and transfer the connectors. Only attempt this with power isolated at the consumer unit, not just the cooker switch, and only if you're comfortable doing it.
• Confirming which element is faulty properly requires an insulation resistance test. A multimeter can catch some faults, but not always the ones that only appear when hot.
• If you're not confident, an appliance engineer can usually diagnose and fit the part in one visit. At 9 years old, a £20 element plus labour is usually still worth it compared with a new built-in oven.

If you tell me the model number (on the sticker around the door frame) and which function makes it trip, I can help you identify the likely part.

It's the big switch labelled RCD with the test button that trips, and nothing else. The fan oven setting trips it every time, but I ran the grill on its own for 10 minutes once and it didn't trip. There's been no burning smell, bang or sparks. I can't see the model number with the door shut, only a faint 'SI6' something.

## Prime suspect: the fan oven element

Your results narrow it down well:

• RCD trips, nothing else → earth leakage, not overload or a dead short
• Grill is fine → the supply, cabling, isolator and grill element are probably OK
• Fan oven trips every time, after a few minutes → the circular element behind the rear panel is most likely, with the fan motor as the runner-up

No bang, smell or sparks also fits: a leaking element usually fails quietly.

## One test to separate element from fan motor

Look for a defrost setting (usually a snowflake symbol), which runs the fan with no heat.

• Runs 15-20 minutes without tripping → fan motor is fine, so it's almost certainly the element
• Trips → fan motor (or its wiring) is the likely culprit

## Finding the model number

On Hotpoint built-ins the rating plate is usually on the edge of the oven frame or cavity, visible with the door open. Check the left or right side of the opening and the edges of the door itself. It'll read something like SI6 864 SH IX. You need the full model and ideally the serial number to order the correct part, as element fittings vary between versions.

## Fixing it

• Part: a replacement fan oven element is usually inexpensive and widely available for Hotpoint models.
• DIY: quite doable if you're handy. You remove the rear fan cover inside the oven, which is held by a few screws. On some models the element terminals are reached from inside. On others the oven has to come out of its housing to reach the connections at the back, which is heavier and more awkward.
• Engineer: if you're not comfortable with that, it's a routine, fairly quick job, and you can tell them exactly what you've found.

If you do it yourself: switch off at the cooker isolator and the cooker MCB in the consumer unit before touching anything, and photograph the wiring before disconnecting it.

## Safety (finishing my earlier note)

• Stop using the fan oven setting until it's repaired. Repeatedly resetting means repeatedly putting current through a leak to earth.
• The RCD is doing exactly its job, so don't be tempted to bypass it or swap circuits around.
• The grill seems OK for now, so using it carefully is reasonable in the meantime. If it ever trips the RCD too, stop using the oven entirely.
• If the defrost test points to the fan motor, or a new element doesn't cure it, get an engineer to check the wiring and fan properly.

I haven't tried a defrost setting and I'm not sure whether this oven has one, so I can't tell you how that would go. I'm not willing to take the back panel off or work inside the oven, and I can't pull it out of its housing on my own because it's screwed in and too heavy. Is there anything else I can check from the front?

Yes, there are a few safe checks you can do from the front without tools. Keep them to a minimum, though. Each trip means the fault is leaking current to earth, so don't keep resetting just to experiment.

## 1. Check the controls for a fan-only setting

Look at the function knob or display for:
• A snowflake symbol (defrost)
• A fan symbol on its own, with no circle or lines around it

If you find one, run it for 15-20 minutes:
• No trip → fan motor is fine, so the element is almost certainly the fault
• Trip → fan motor or its wiring

If there's no such setting, skip this. The element is still the most likely cause.

## 2. Find the rating plate

Open the door and look around the edges of the oven frame, the sides of the cavity opening, and the inner edge of the door. You're looking for a sticker with the full model (e.g. SI6 8xx...) and serial number. Photograph it. This is the most useful thing you can give an engineer or parts supplier.

## 3. Look at the element through the fan cover

With the oven cold and off, shine a torch through the slots in the rear fan cover. You may be able to see part of the circular element. Look for:
• Blistering, bulges or cracks in the metal
• Discoloured or burnt spots
• Any section that looks split or sagging

You won't always see damage, since insulation breakdown is often invisible, but if you do spot it, that confirms the diagnosis.

## 4. Check for moisture

Has anything recently spilled or boiled over, or have you used a lot of liquid cleaner or steam cleaning? Is there water in the base of the cavity? Moisture can cause or worsen leakage. If so, wipe it dry and leave the door open for a day. It occasionally helps temporarily, but an element that trips every time usually needs replacing.

## 5. Reduce other load on that RCD (optional, one try)

RCDs trip on the total leakage across all circuits they protect. Switch off or unplug other appliances on that half of the house (washing machine, kettle, fridge if practical, etc.), then try the fan oven once. If it still trips, the oven is leaking enough on its own. If it doesn't, the oven is still the main suspect, but other appliances are adding to it.

## Next step: book an engineer

You've done the useful diagnosis already. Tell them:
> "Hotpoint built-in oven, model [from rating plate], about 9 years old. The fan oven setting trips the RCD after a few minutes, every time. The grill works fine. No smell or bang. I suspect the fan oven element."

That should mean a quick visit, and many engineers will bring the likely part. On a 9-year-old oven, replacing an element is normally well worth it compared with buying a new built-in oven.

## Safety (finishing my earlier note)

• Don't use the fan oven until it's repaired. The grill seems OK to use for now, but stop if it trips.
• Don't keep resetting the RCD to test things. It's protecting you from a genuine fault.
• If you ever notice burning smells, scorch marks, a hot isolator switch, or the RCD tripping with the oven off, switch off at the cooker isolator and call an electrician.
